newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crude demand thin, prices meltdown.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crude demand thin, prices meltdown.

text.p: U.S. refiners were hugging the sides watching prices for delivered crudes meltdown as sellers in long positions had trouble attracting buyers.
European and West African crude markets continued to be hit by ample supplies but traders said the import window into the U.S. was still far from profitable.
A swathe of North Sea cargoes threatened to send premiums lower, which thinned even the U.S. domestic market.
"Why would anyone want to buy when prices are falling? WTI at $25 (a barrel) was ridiculous," an East Coast trader said, noting recently firm Louisiana prices were already softening.
A European trader with one remaining Brent on its ULCC was reported to have offered Brent at West Texas Intermediate +25 cents cif for mid-Nov early Wednesday.
The offer was later heard revised to +15 cents cif amid lukewarm interest and other competing supplies.
Light Norwegian and Colombian crudes were seen available, but prices were obscured by thin discussion.
In nearby markets, Oriente for late Nov was valued at WTI -$2.60-70 a barrel cif, fluctuating around recent weak levels.
Few other South American cargoes were heard, except for a parcel of Vasconia pegged around WTI -$2.00 for late Nov.
Chile's state oil company ENAP, meanwhile, said it aimed to issue a purchase tender for Dec some time next week.
Brent trade in the U.S. after-market was deathly quiet with outright and intermonth levels stagnant near their London levels.
Dec Brent stood at $23.55-60 a barrel, with Dec/Jan modestly higher at 39/43 cents.
